📍America's inflation expectations have become tied to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab

🔖In a tweet, Ghalibaf preemptively dismissed today's much-hyped decision by the US central bank on interest rates as inconsequential regardless of its outcome, writing:

📌Let's see whether the Federal Reserve can open the Strait of Hormuz or produce even one more barrel of oil by raising interest rates?!

📌You can't manage (anchor) inflation expectations in America by raising and lowering interest rates, because those expectations are driven by the supply-side shock caused by the blockage of energy chokepoints — namely the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and have nothing to do with interest rates. It is the "Strait of Hormuz risk" that determines the rate, and control over that risk now lies with Iran.

📌Ghalibaf's emphasis in this post is on the idea that the era of managing inflation and inflation expectations using demand-side tools alone (interest rates) is over, and that it is geopolitics that now holds the upper hand in shaping economic indicators such as inflation.

📌Under normal conditions, a central bank traditionally seeks to anchor inflation expectations to its inflation target or to a credible long-term inflation rate in order to contain inflation, and it achieves this anchoring by adjusting interest rates in line with the inflation target and the economy's distance from full capacity.

📌But in this post, the Parliament Speaker, by upending the classic formula for setting interest rates in America, warns market participants that tinkering with interest rates will not achieve the goal of containing inflation in America, and that they must factor new variables into their calculations — such as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab — and accept that circumstances have changed: unless Iran wills it, inflation expectations in America will not be anchorable, and inflation will keep climbing.
